📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Amazon rainforest plays a key part in the cycling of carbon and water on regional and global scales, and is widely viewed as a perennially evergreen ecosystem. However, writing in Nature, Song et al.1 report that there are extended periods when trees in most of the rainforest remain leafless. Known as deciduousness, this state occurs between the shedding of old leaves and the emergence and early development (flushing) of fresh ones. The authors also found that hydroclimatic conditions such as annual rainfall have a more crucial role in determining this pattern of leaf behaviour than do soil properties and light availability. The seasonal variation in tropical leaf cover and photosynthetic activity in the Amazon observed by the authors is less pronounced than that seen for broadleaf trees in temperate and boreal climate zones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well-known former Chelsea, Barcelona and Liverpool players are among the major names to have retired in 2026.

Time is a curse for a football fan, as a host of players we have watched for major periods of their career call it a day and hang up their boots.

We’ve looked into 18 players who have called it a day in 2026.

Berahino has retired from football at 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi’s national team.

Recent findings suggest that it feels like a long time ago that he scored 20 goals in league and cup for West Brom in 2014-15. That made Berahino hot property, with Spurs seriously keen before plumping for Son Heung-min instead.

The striker never did capture that form again, faltering with the Baggies before a disastrous £12 million move to Stoke in 2017.

Berhaino has since played for Charlton and Sheffield Wednesday, before spells in Cyprus, India and Slovenia.

Pedro ends his playing career as one of the most decorated players in modern football, having won the World Cup and Euros with Spain alongside a plethora of trophies at club level.

The forward was part of Pep Guardiola’s glittering Barcelona side, before scoring 43 goals in 206 Chelsea appearances.

He left to join Roma in 2020, before becoming the first player since 1985 to move between the two Rome rivals when he signed for Lazio in the following year.

Pedro remained at Lazio until his decision to retire at the age of 39.

After a glittering career, including World Cup glory in 2014 and 49 goals for Germany, Podolski called it a day in May 2026.

The 40-year-old represented several European giants throughout his career, including Bayern Munich, Inter Milan, Galatasaray and Arsenal.

He ended his career with boyhood club Gornik Zabrze in Poland and even skippered them to cup glory in his final campaign.

Borini played for Chelsea and Liverpool in the early-2010s, but is still beloved at Sunderland for his relegation-dodging goals under Gus Poyet and Sam Allardyce.

Recent findings suggest that the forward left Wearside in 2018, spending time in exotic locations like Milan, deepest Turkey and Salford. He retired in October 2026.

Former Arsenal, Swansea and West Ham goalkeeper Fabianski has hung up his gloves at the age of 41.

But Fabianski has no intention of quitting the game entirely, announcing his prepares to work with the next generation of goalkeepers in a coaching role.

No Premier League player has ever made more appearances than Milner, who broke Gareth Barry’s long-standing record in February 2026.

The midfielder made his Leeds debut in 2002, sharing a pitch with sepia-toned names like Nigel Winterburn and Lucas Radebe.

His career with Leeds, Aston Villa, Newcastle, Manchester City, Liverpool, Brighton and England was nothing less than stellar and Milner called it a day this year at the age of 40.

started his career at Cardiff City before a 2008 move to Arsenal, where he won three FA Cups – scoring the winning goal in two of those finals – during his 11 years with the Gunners.

He then had spells with Juventus, Nice, Rangers, a second stint at Cardiff and Pumas UNAM before ending his career in April.

Ramsey is now manager of League One side Oxford United.

One of the biggest sh*thouses in recent football history, Costa was a menace during his days with Atletico Madrid and Chelsea.

He played his last professional match in 2024, but it wasn’t until earlier this year when he appeared on a podcast that he confirmed his retirement.

Oscar was just 25 when he signed for Shanghai Port, leaving Chelsea for a £60million fee and plenty of raised eyebrows.

The Brazilian spent seven years in China to the glee of his bank manager, although a player of such talent should really have been playing in a more competitive league.

Sources indicate that he spent the last few months of his career at Sao Paulo, before retiring in April. This was due to a heart condition which led to him collapsing and requiring CPR in a training session.

Young brought the curtain down on an exceptional 23-year career in May, retiring at the age of 40 after a final season with Ipswich Town in the Championship.

Starting as a winger with Watford and Aston Villa, Young gradually became a defender during his Manchester United days and won a Serie A title with Inter Milan in 2021.

He was also an crucial member of England’s 2018 World Cup squad.

One of the biggest ‘Streets Won’t Forget’ footballers in Premier League history after his spell at West Ham in the mid-2010s, Payet retired earlier this year.

In a recent development, the French playmaker spent the final years of his playing days at Vasco de Gama, still capable of scoring outrageous free-kicks. A maverick in an increasingly systemised sport.

Most famously associated with Leicester’s 2016 title win, Schmeichel retired in May 2026 after suffering a shoulder injury a few months previously.

Then with Celtic, it was expected that Schemeichel’s surgery would keep him out of action for up to a year anyway.

Aged 39, the son of legendary goalkeeper Peter enjoyed a hugely successful career in his own right.

A loyal servant at Chelsea between 2012 and 2023, Azpilicueta ended his career in May after helping Sevilla avoid relegation.

The full-back made over 500 appearances for Chelsea, the sixth most in the club’s history, and appeared as a BBC pundit during the World Cup.

An eight-times capped Netherlands international, Van Ginkel represented substantial clubs like Chelsea and AC Milan, but his careers at both clubs were short.

In England, he also played for Stoke, but the midfielder featured in his home country for the majority of his career, playing more than 100 games for both PSV Eindhoven and Vitesse.

At 33 years of age, Van Ginkel has hung up his boots.

Pjanic had a very successful career at club level, playing for giants such as Roma, Juventus and Barcelona.

The Bosnian won seven trophies with Juve, one with Barca and was named Roma’s footballer of the year in 2014.

At international level, he’ll go down as a legend, having represented his country over 100 times, while he contributed to two goals in his three World Cup games.

Pjanic technically retired in the final days of 2025, but who cares for such semantics? Any excuse for us to relive his glory days at Lyon.

Sakho left Paris Saint-Germain for a Liverpool team which wasn’t particularly good while he was there, and in doing so ended his spell of winning trophies: four at PSG and not a single one in his career after that.

The Reds finished second in Sakho’s first campaign there, before slipping to sixth and then eighth in the Premier League for the following two seasons.

Sakho was on the club’s books as they finished fourth the next season, though he was on loan at Crystal Palace when that happened.

He would move permanently to Palace, netting Liverpool a healthy fee, then back to France with Montpellier, before his final spell in professional football with Torpedo Kutaisi in Georgia.

Mata finished his career playing in Australia, leaving Melbourne Victory in September before confirming his retirement in November.

The Spaniard starred for Chelsea and Manchester United in the Premier League in his prime after coming through the Real Madrid academy and making his name at Valencia.

A World Cup winner with Spain in 2010 and a member of their triumphant Euro 2012 squad, Mata is now bowing out at the age of 38.

A three-time Europa League winner with Sevilla, Banega was clearly eager not to just be remembered as the guy who ran over his own foot at a petrol station.

The midfielder had a 10-year international career with Argentina and was most recently playing back in his homeland with Defensa y Justicia.

Recent findings suggest that but at the age of 38, he’s saying enough is enough. “Even if Messi calls me for Inter Miami, I would tell him no,” insisted Banega, who also noted he wouldn’t want to “take the place” of young players trying to break through at clubs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 06:08 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 03:22 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • The Premier League have ruled that referees made a staggering six incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.
  • It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 06:08 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 03:22 EST, 19 November 2026.

The Premier League have ruled that referees made a staggering six incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.

It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.

That is because the laws state that if a foul occurs before an offside offence, a penalty should be awarded.

Although Havertz was in an offside position, he had not committed an offence as he neither played the ball nor interfered with play.

The key match incidents panel (KMI) said: 'Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded.'.

Farai Hallam's decision not to award Kai Havertz a penalty was deemed incorrect by the key match incidents panel.

Coventry were wrongly denied a spot-kick in their defeat to Everton after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

In a recent development, 1. Everton vs Coventry City: Frank Lampard's side should have been awarded a penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

In a recent development, 2. Everton vs Coventry City: The Toffees' second goal, scored by Thierno Barry should not have stood as the ball was adjudged to have gone into the back of the net off his hand.

According to recent reports, 3. Arsenal vs Hull City: Kai Havertz was denied a penalty after being dragged down. The referee did not award a spot-kick because Havertz in an offside position. However, that decision was incorrect, as he was not committing an offside offence and a spot-kick should therefore have been awarded.

4. Crystal Palace vs Liverpool: Palace were awarded a penalty in the last minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool after Milos Kerkez and Dario Osario clashed heads in the penalty area. The panel saw this as a natural coming together.

It has been revealed that 5. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: A penalty was given after Abdoul Ouattara tumbled over. The referee gave a foul against Lewis Cook despite Ouattara stepping across him.

Industry observers note that 6. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: Marcus Tavernier should have seen a second yellow card for time-wasting.

They did, however, praise the VAR for asking the referee to review the incident on the monitor, even though Hallam stuck with his on-field call after watching it back.

In the same weekend, Tottenham Hotspur complained to Pro Ref after Jayden Bogle's heavy challenge on Mathys Tel's ankle, which forced him off injured.

Spurs felt Bogle should have seen red, particularly after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar incident the week prior.

Reviewing the decision, the KMI panel were split but eventually concluded that the foul lacked 'the speed, force or intensity' to be considered serious foul play.

Two of the five panellists, however, felt that the challenge merited a red card.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's consolation penalty in the 92nd minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool should never have been awarded.

The KMI panel unanimously agreed the referee was wrong to award a penalty when Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio clashed heads while contesting the ball, with contact inevitable given both players were jumping.

However, VAR's decision not to intervene was supported because it was not a 'clear and obvious error'.

It is the second penalty incident in as many weeks that went against Liverpool after Alexander Isak was wrongfully denied a spot-kick against Arsenal.

It has been revealed that on the opposite side of Merseyside, James Tarkowski was fortunate not to concede a penalty for pulling Caleb Yirenkyi's hair during Everton's win over Coventry City, with the score still 0-0 at the time. The panel found that Coventry should have been awarded a penalty while Tarkowski should have been booked.

Industry observers note that last season, that incident would likely have resulted in a straight red card. However, the guidance changed this term with red cards only brandished for excessive force.

Thierno Barry's goal that gave Everton the lead faced scrutiny as three panellists believed it should have been disallowed on the pitch, with the 'balance of probability suggesting the ball accidentally struck Barry's hand before directly entering the goal'.

There were also two incorrect decisions in Bournemouth's victory over Ipswich Town.

Bournemouth defender Marcus Tavernier should have been sent off for a second yellow card in the 96th minute for delaying the restart during their 2-1 win, the panel found. However, it was a close call as the panel voted 3-2 against the decision.

Ipswich's scored penalty was also deemed wrongly awarded, with Abdoul Ouattara stepping across Lewis Cook to win the spot-kick rather than being fouled by the defender.

The KMI panel consists of a representative from the Premier League and Pro Ref alongside three former managers or players and meets after every round of Premier League matches to evaluate significant refereeing decisions.

Ref boss Howard Webb will speak to Premier League clubs at a routine meeting on Thursday.

While the panel is not new, this is the first season their findings have been publicly released in Pro Ref's drive for greater transparency and accountability.

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb is due to appear in front of clubs on Thursday at a routine Premier League meeting.

And in more positive news for Webb, he will be able to share that VAR delays are down this season after increasing the bar for interventions.

Meanwhile, the KMI panel have assessed 296 decisions this season - only six of which have been judged to be wrong post-VAR.

6 times players came back to haunt their old club ahead of Bruno Guimaraes’ Newcastle return

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bruno Guimaraes is the latest Premier League player to return to a former club as Arsenal take on Newcastle United, but will the Brazilian follow in the footsteps of others and get a goal?
  • From apologising to full-length runs of the pitch, players scoring against their old clubs results in a number of different reactions.
  • Here are six of the best of them from Premier League history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Guimaraes is the latest Premier League player to return to a former club as Arsenal take on Newcastle United, but will the Brazilian follow in the footsteps of others and get a goal?

From apologising to full-length runs of the pitch, players scoring against their old clubs results in a number of different reactions.

Here are six of the best of them from Premier League history.

We’re generally against players not celebrating goals against former clubs but when that player has played 648 times for them, perhaps we can understand it.

Lampard’s move from Chelsea to Fresh York City came with an unexpected stopping-over point of Manchester City where of course he scored against his former club.

It was at the Etihad and City were trailing thanks to a goal from Andre Schurrle when Lampard scored an equaliser five minutes from time.

He looked like a dog that had just eaten something he knows he shouldn’t have as he put a single hand up in the air to apologise.

Rooney’s departure from Everton was a little messy with Everton fans chanting against him even as he was still their player and that bitterness was still there three years later.

In 2007, United trailed Everton 2-0 which gave the home fans the confidence to give their old player a bit of stick.

But it was a case of kicking the bear. United levelled in the 68th minute after Phil Neville put the ball in his own net and 11 minutes from time, Rooney grabbed the winner.

And there was certainly no lack of a celebration.

After a few bounces like a man who could not decide what to do, Rooney looked the Goodison Park faithful in the eye and kissed the United badge.

Would Wayne Rooney have worked in Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona?

It is the absolute gold standard of blood-boiling celebrations.

Adebayor was annoyed at Arsenal for what he felt was Arsene Wenger forcing him out, resulting in a £25.5m move to Manchester City.

Wenger suggested it was more a need to raise money but Adebayor took it to heart and let his emotions come out when the two clubs next met.

In a recent development, he netted in a 4-2 win and sprinted the full length of the pitch to taunt the travelling Arsenal fans. Referee Mark Clattenburg looked like a disappointed parent while stewards struggled to hold the enraged Arsenal fans back.

According to recent reports, it was not Adebayor’s only moment of the game either. He stamped on Robin van Persie’s face, landing him a retrospective three-match ban, and even got into arguments with Cesc Fabregas and Alex Song.

Ince had controversially made his way to Liverpool having previously spent six years at United and he rubbed salt into the wound in 1999.

A few weeks before United would go on to lift the treble, Ince scored a late equaliser at Anfield and celebrated by hugging about six different fans in the stands.

The goal and result looked to have swung the title race to Arsenal but United did eventually lift the trophy.

Van Persie was enemy number one around the Emirates in 2012 after he left for Manchester United and he acknowledged that fact when he scored in the first three minutes when they met at Old Trafford in the 2012/13 season.

He gave a double-handed apology and looked genuinely disheartened by the goal. In the away leg, he scored once more but again refused to celebrate.

Six months on though and Van Persie very much did celebrate.

He rose well to meet a Wayne Rooney corner and went full knee slide in his celebration. As he was hugging Rooney, his face did though look like a man who’s just remembered he was supposed to not celebrate.

It’s not one of the more well-known names but we are including it because it led to a rule change.

LuaLua was on loan at Portsmouth from Newcastle at a time when there was no restriction on when loan players could feature.

In a recent development, newcastle were winning 1-0 away at Fratton Park when guess who scored to equalise it. Bearing in mind he was still an employee at this point, LuaLua celebrated by taking his shirt off in what is possibly the furthest thing away from an apology.

Newcastle manager Bobby Robson said: “He was the last player we wanted to score against us. One of our players has taken a point off us.”.

That bizarre situation led to the Premier League tweaking the rules to prevent loaned players from facing their parent club.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 20, 2010, Tottenham Hotspur played their part in one of the most memorable North London derbies in history with a 3-2 comeback victory over Arsenal. How well do you remember that side?

It has been revealed that to jog your memory: goals from Samir Nasri and Marouane Chamakh (of all people) gave the Gunners a two-goal lead within the opening half an hour. But Spurs raced back with three second-half goals to register their first win away at Arsenal in 17 years.

“I gave them a rollicking at half-time, and woke them up a bit,” Harry Redknapp said afterwards.

Sources indicate that “We took the game to them from the start of the second half. We had to go for broke. It wasn’t a case of trying to stem the tide, it was a case of trying to get back into the game.

“We were either going to get beat 5-0, or have a go. That’s what we did, because that’s my nature.”.

It has been revealed that he added: “We can beat anybody. This has put us right back in the race again. It’s wide open. “If my players believe in themselves as much as I do, we can achieve anything.”.

Spurs went on to finish fifth but that shouldn’t detract from a famous victory at the Emirates.

We’re asking you to name the 11 players that Redknapp chose in his starting line-up that afternoon. The time to beat from the Planet Football office is 01:34 but any Spurs fans worth their salt will fancy their chances of beating us.

Tech Report: Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Industry observers note that eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

In a recent development, “You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”.

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and mentioned “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM.

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

Recent findings suggest that so while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

According to recent reports, the anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”.

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Sources indicate that salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

It has been revealed that FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL.

As the home fans set off flares, filling the air with plumes of thick, red smoke, the theme tune to Captain Pugwash was played. Arteta tried to find answers from his coaching staff, amid the cacophony, but occasionally you do not have to look too deep for answers.

It has been revealed that could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

Recent findings suggest that so it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Viktor Gyökeres gets his first goal of the season and Arsenal are level against Fleetwood! 🔴 https://t.co/LfZcIbAfCX.

A game of attack against defence played out for the remainder before Dowman was harshly dismissed in the 85th minute after reacting to a tough challenge from Neal. There was still time for Fleetwood’s Lynch to make two excellent saves from White and Odegaard in added time as Arsenal tried to avoid the shoot-out lottery. They could not and how it hurt them.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ.

“Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and removed,” Matt Lawlor, the Fleetwood manager, mentioned. “To me, there was that feeling we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special.

“To be giving that to football fans and especially Fleetwood fans is unbelievably special. I’m really proud of it. Football’s a funny old game, isn’t it?”.

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players. I haven’t seen anyone not doing what is required at this level. But, obviously, we insisted so much, we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, obviously, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t. And football is about that.

Attitude wise, absolutely zero [wrong] otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way. It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline.

Something that we discussed already before the match.

It’s difficult to see on the cameras, I prefer to watch it back properly and I will assess the situation.

We will learn from everything [on if he will learn from it].

I don’t think it will [sink in], it’s really hard to address the players when we have a league game on Saturday and I didn’t want to be the bearer of reality. The biggest night in the club’s history. We’ve beaten the champions, somehow!

We knew before the game, we’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to go to the best team in the country and the most organised team in the country and the best of the basics and the world-class players, in that we’re going to go and outplay them. So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them. And I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.

Obviously, the goal happens, but they’re going to happen; they’re so good at football. The footballers that they have, the gaps that they find and we see it every week in the Premier League.

To beat the English champions on penalties, credit to everyone one of these lads. We looked at Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We compared it even though these are the champions. We thought ‘if we lay it all out there, let’s see what happens.

'They get lost in it, it’s an engaging distraction, and it satisfies their competitive edge, but just like mindlessly scrolling YouTube or social media, you need to put your own filters and blockers in place, otherwise you’ll find yourself doing something ridiculously stupid and playing for hours and hours, hurting your performance,' he told Ozoon.

The pair become embroiled in a Bonnie and Clyde-style crime story after 'an easy score goes wrong', leaving them 'forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive'.

Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many giant viruses can be seen under a light microscope.Credit: Gabrielle Voinot/Eurelios/Look at Sciences/SPL.
  • Roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts.
  • Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so massive that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many giant viruses can be seen under a light microscope.Credit: Gabrielle Voinot/Eurelios/Look at Sciences/SPL.

Roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts. Microbiologists say that these ‘egoviruses’ could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly. The findings are published in Nature1.

Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so massive that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.

Poxviruses are an outlier in the giant-virus world because they can directly infect humans and animals and their origin is a mystery, says Fasséli Coulibaly, a structural biologist at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. Egoviruses could be the evolutionary bridge between microorganism-infecting giant viruses called asfuviruses and pathogenic poxviruses, he says.

In a recent development, tom Delmont, a microbial ecologist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research in Paris, and his colleagues discovered egoviruses while combing through online libraries of metagenomes. These contain the genetic information of all the organisms in a particular environment, which means that researchers can hunt for microbes without having to cultivate them. When the team scanned for a single gene found in most nucleocytoviruses, they discovered egoviruses — the only type of nucleocytovirus that is prevalent in the gut.

In a recent development, they found egovirus DNA in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people. One of these clades is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the global population, on the basis of the presence of at least one of two egovirus proteins in the samples they analysed.

It has been revealed that the researchers detected these proteins in samples spanning a large proportion of the human population, from the Hadza, a hunter-gatherer group in Tanzania, to populations in Europe, the United States and South America, claims Delmont. That suggests that egoviruses have been inhabiting the human gut for a long time, he adds.

Sources indicate that that egoviruses are found in many animal species, including people, and are widespread around the world shows that giant viruses are more diverse than previously thought, says Subir Sarker, a molecular virologist at James Cook University in Townsville, Queensland. “This is a really groundbreaking study,” he adds.

To identify potential hosts for egoviruses in the gut, the team compared the amount of genetic overlap between egoviruses and organisms with a nucleus. The researchers found the most overlap with single-celled organisms that help ruminants, such as cows, to digest their food.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was born in North Wales in 1980, and my first memory of football was playing for the school team as a kid.

As a nine or 10-year-old I started getting my cousin’s hand-me-down Everton shirts, and this certainly helped me decide which of the local sides I was going to follow!

The two red sides close by (Wrexham and the other lot) never once turned my head.

And then, in 1991, my mind was made up for good. My uncle asked me if I’d like to go to watch Everton play.

It was the first ever game I’d been to watch live. It was at Bramall Lane, and I’ll never ever forget it.

My uncle got us to the ground early and took me and my cousin to wait for the players’ coach to turn up.

The coach arrived and as I was only a little kid at that point, my uncle lifted me up to get a glimpse of the players.

The first player I saw was big Neville Southall and I reached over to pat him on the back and wish him good luck. He glanced over his shoulder and gave me a wry smile.

Not only was I now hooked on Everton, but all I wanted to be from that point on was a goalkeeper.

Recent findings suggest that A few years later I got to taste my first ever trophy win as an Evertonian. Me and my dad watched the whole FA Cup final build-up from Grandstand in the morning to Match of the Day, with the game in between.

We couldn’t get tickets to the final, but my uncle and cousin did go the Charity Shield.

Even though that was my last taste of silverware as an Evertonian, my love for this club has never wavered.

I’m now 46 years old, lived in Australia for 20 years and I’m happily married with seven children – six of which have all been to Goodison and the youngest has beat me to visit the upcoming stadium last year!

My highlights of the last 35 years are:.

-              - My first game in 1991.

-              - 1995 and the FA Cup victory.

-              - Going to Howard’s testimonial a few months before leaving for Australia.

-              - Spending a day painting parts of Goodison in 2013.

-              - Goodison trips with my dad, cousins, uncle and taking my six kids to see the eventual champions in 2016.

-              -Taking my two sons to the games in Sydney.

-              - My daughter (who now lives in Rochdale) going to the last game at Goodison.

-              - And my wife taking our two youngest daughters to see our stone at the upcoming ground last year.

I’ve got so many fond memories of our beautiful club, and I can’t wait to make millions more in the coming decades.

It has been revealed that there is no other football club for me or my family. Once a Blue, always a Blue.

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 08:14 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 10:33 EST, 19 November 2026.

Manchester United have released their latest financial results after spending another £15million to install Mauricio Pochettino as the club’s fresh head coach.

United’s first quarter financials up to September 30 don’t include the cost of paying the US Soccer Federation £10m to buy Pochettino and his backroom staff out of their contracts, or an additional £5m to pay off Michael Carrick and his staff.

They show that United brought in total revenues of £146.1m compared to £140.3m in the first quarter last year, but made an operating loss for the quarter of £3m compared with an operating profit of £13m 12 months ago.

The results come just weeks after co-owner Avram Glazer told a conference that the club’s value is not dependent on success on the pitch.

Sources say that United acted early in the season to address the drop in form under Carrick that saw United slide into the relegation zone, and the club are now focused on improving results under Pochettino.

The Argentine is expected to be given a modest transfer budget in January to make fresh signings, with United in the market for a striker, left-back and centre-back.

Man United's latest financial results come after the Glazers mentioned that success isn't dependent on results.

The results don't include the £10m United paid to buy Pochettino and his staff from the US national team.

Chief executive Omar Berrada mentioned: ‘Our revenue remains strong and on track, while we continue to grow sustainably. We are pleased to welcome Mauricio Pochettino and his staff to the club and our priority is to support them as we look continuously to improve our performances on the pitch.’.

Sources indicate that the latest results only cover the first five Premier League fixtures of the season, one Champions League match and the League Cup defeat to Brighton. Sources insist that they show the benefit of the cost-cutting under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos and what they say is improved operational efficiency.

United have reiterated their guidance of total revenues of £740-£760m for this financial year after reporting that the first quarter saw rises in broadcast (£5.3m), retail (£1.3m) and matchday (£0.6m) revenues.

However, sponsorship revenue was down by £1.4m despite a latest training kit deal with Betway, largely due to United playing individual pre-season friendlies rather than going on summer tour.

Employee benefit expenses for the quarter were £79.9m, an increase of £6.3m due mainly to players' wages going up 25 per cent after qualifying for the Champions League.

United's borrowing has increased 19 per cent from a year ago, with the club's historic US dollar debt up $125m to $775m 'as a result of the refinancing of our senior secured notes in June 2026'.

Sources indicate that this rise, which was revealed in the last set of results in September, equates to £577.4m, up from £481.2m. The net cost of financing that debt dropped from £21.4m to £14.5m.

Meanwhile, United’s borrowing on the club's revolving credit facility was £207.1m as of September 30, down from £268m a year ago.

The Santos star, 34, raised hell at Coritiba fans following his side's 1-0 win over them on Wednesday, with the climax of the Brazilian season approaching.

'Suck it! You have to respect me, respect me, you f****** small team.'.

And this is not the first time Neymar has vented his spleen this season.

Neymar branded Coritiba a 'small f****** team' in a rant at rival supporters who taunted him.

Earlier this season, he was involved in a furious altercation with rival officials in the tunnel.

In August, he was involved in a furious altercation with Remo officials after Santos beat them in the last 16 of the Brazilian Cup.

The Brazilian football icon screamed inside the tunnel as he was drawn into a heated exchange with Remo's directors.

He repeatedly shouted the word 'eliminated' before taunting the rivals with a series of gestures at his dressing room's entrance.

Despite his bragging over other teams, it has been a distinctly average campaign for Santos so far.

Santos sit eighth in the Brazilian Serie A and, despite him telling Coritiba that they will go down, that looks unlikely with the southern side sat 13th out of 20 with four games to go, four points above the drop zone.

Meanwhile, while he mocked Remo over being eliminated from the cup, Santos went out in the quarter-finals 3-0 on aggregate to Palmeiras.

Neymar has had a fairly effective season personally, scoring 10 goals and recording eight assists in all competitions while captaining Santos.

It remains to be seen whether he will play beyond the end of his contract in December, but the club's chief executive, who happens to be Neymar's dad, certainly wants to extend his son's term.

Industry observers note that 'We know that in every transfer window, offers come in for him to leave. Yet Neymar always chooses to stay at Santos. What I'm anticipating is that, first and foremost, I need to keep Neymar happy. Do you understand?' he said.

'And if he's happy here, I can keep him here. So, look, down this final stretch, the work we've done to structure the squad and open up positive possibilities has given us the license to dream.'.

Neymar, who was widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of his generation during his time at Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain, returned to his boyhood club Santos from Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal in January 2025.

His £200million move from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain remains the most expensive transfer of all time.

In June he made his first appearance for Brazil since 2023 after rupturing his ACL and meniscus in his left knee.

The Everton defender made his second successive start of this international window as his nation claimed all three points, while fellow Blues Brennan Johnson and Jake O’Brien were also in action for their respective countries.

Recent findings suggest that it is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

It has been revealed that “There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola mentioned ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”.

Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

In a recent development, “We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso mentioned. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”.

Published: 11:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 11:59 EST, 19 November 2026.

One of football’s largest financial lenders abandoned a planned £1.5billion loan to Manchester City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

The decision by US private capital group Apollo Global Management is the latest evidence that the money markets deem City a financial risk, as the club prepare an appeal against their conviction on the vast majority of 115 Premier League charges of inflating income through sham contracts.

According to recent reports, it was reported by Bloomberg last week that a German lender, Oldenburgische Landesbank (OL), had pulled out of a deal that would have let Brazilian top-flight side Palmeiras take a large upfront payment against instalments City are due to pay them for midfielder Allan Elias, signed this summer for £32million with £2m add-ons. That bank views City as a reputational and financial risk.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Apollo was in the final stages of negotiating the loan to City Football Group (CFG) in September, when the deal collapsed after the ruling that they artificially inflated their financial position to the tune of more than £900m over nine years.

According to recent reports, city owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan injected £100m into the club in the month after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Mansour, who has only been present at one City home game since Abu Dhabi bought the club in 2008, has made no public comment on the club’s conviction, which delivers huge reputational damage to his image-conscious country.

In a recent development, there are signs that football is preparing for a strong legal attack from Abu Dhabi if City lose their appeal. Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors in the event of sponsors Etihad and Etisalat suing them, it was also revealed on Thursday. Legal indemnity will be in place for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittain and three other non-executive directors.

US private capital group Apollo Global Management abandoned a £1.5billion loan to Man City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

City owner Sheikh Mansou injected £100m into the club after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi.

But the refusal of credit by Apollo, which has loaned £80m to Premier League football club Nottingham Forest and has a minority stake in Championship side Wrexham, demonstrates that the capital markets think City are imperilled, with the appeal process by no means straightforward.

Recent findings suggest that if an appeal failed, City could seek a judicial review of the commission's findings at the High Court. But to do so, they would need to demonstrate that the Premier League acted outside its powers or reached a conclusion which no reasonable authority could have reached. City would need the High Court’s permission to make a judicial review application and the bar is high.

Financial analyst Paul Quinn wrote on The Esk website that Apollo’s problem had been with City, not Abu Dhabi itself. Three weeks ago, Apollo agreed to take a minority stake in Mubadala Capital, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund chaired by Sheikh Mansour and run by City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak. Apollo and City have not commented.

Quinn said that CFG needed the money because it was not self-funding, despite City’s financial strength. CFG’s pre-tax loss widened from £122.2m to £292.3m in the last financial year. City produced £694.1m of CFG’s £888m group revenue and ran up a £9m loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Q: Jarrad, it’s still early in the season, but from your perspective, how is it going?

It’s going well. As a team, we’re in a positive place, especially after the recent results. It’s put us in a good position in the Cup and the Premier League.

Q: With how well it’s going in the league and the Carabao Cup, does it feel like there’s a lot of quality in this Everton squad?

I think the players we’ve got and the quality in the team is probably one of the best we’ve had over the past few seasons.

The squad isn’t as massive as other squads, but the quality we have is definitely up there.

I think we’ve just got to stick together and be resilient.

Q: And after recovering from a hamstring injury last season, how are you feeling?

Good. I’m in a good position. I think the summer and pre-season helped to get me where I am now.

I was managed by staff, managed my load through pre-season, managed my training load.

Sources indicate that so, hopefully, it’s helping. I'm feeling good.

Q: Just how frustrating was it last season?

Last season was tough. It was the first time I’d had a big injury which kept setting me back. When you can’t find a solution to something, it’s frustrating.

You do everything you can and then it sets you back again.

Q: I remember you breaking down against Liverpool and you looked broken. That must’ve been horrible to deal with?

Yeah, I think it was the fourth time it had happened in the same place.

When you’ve tried different things and nothing’s happening, and then for [the injury] to happen again, it was tough.

It’s probably set me back a bit, so I’m trying to make up for the time I’ve lost. I think the start of the season has definitely helped with that.

Sources indicate that Q: What sort of approach did you take in your recovery? I imagine you tried several options.

I spoke to a few players who’ve had similar concerns and reached out to someone in Germany – a specialist there – for a different approach to what I’d been doing, and the Club were on board with it.

I was there for four weeks, and they took me through their procedure, which looked – not just at the hamstring – but how the whole body moves, your brain and how everything moves.

It was a holistic approach and that definitely put me in a better position to come back here, and then with the Club helping me with my load, that put me in a better position.

Q: Are you able to share which other players you spoke to?

In a recent development, mainly Dominic Calvert-Lewin. When he was here, he was struggling with similar challenges, so I reached out to him.

Tom Davies, as well. I reached out to him. They spoke really highly of [the specialist].

I spoke to Merlin (Röhl), and he knew a few people who had been there, so I think it was the right time to get different advice and a different opinion.

Q: But now, you’re feeling in a much better place?

Yeah, I feel in a better position now with the way I’ve been managed, and I feel confident in myself.

I think I feel more confident now coming back and I want to prove to everyone how good I am.

Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.

'If you don't give him what he wants, he'll burn your house down': Inside the 'cult' of Sir Jim Ratcliffe, as sources from his crumbling sporting empire reveal the destructive know-it-all arrogance of Man United co-owner and his henchmen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 12:11 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • The flat rural acres of the Turweston Aerodrome, in the north-west corner of Buckinghamshire, are far enough from human habitation for anyone padlocked in a building out there to feel seriously threatened.
  • The ‘imprisonment’ of the four-time British Olympic champion in a building, with signs declaring ‘No Entry’ fixed to the external doors, was one of the more extraordinary allegations to emerge from the court case, settled this week, over a £180million yacht Ratcliffe and Ainslie built together for the 2024 America’s Cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 12:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 12:11 EST, 19 November 2026.

The flat rural acres of the Turweston Aerodrome, in the north-west corner of Buckinghamshire, are far enough from human habitation for anyone padlocked in a building out there to feel seriously threatened. And if the testimony of Sir Ben Ainslie is to be believed, that’s what can come of crossing swords with Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The ‘imprisonment’ of the four-time British Olympic champion in a building, with signs declaring ‘No Entry’ fixed to the external doors, was one of the more extraordinary allegations to emerge from the court case, settled this week, over a £180million yacht Ratcliffe and Ainslie built together for the 2024 America’s Cup.

Ratcliffe, who had withdrawn financial support, was demanding the team’s assets and intellectual property, and, according to court papers, Ineos representative Raymond Fellows, assisted by two security contractors, arrived at the offices of Ainslie's Athena Racing and applied his own chain and padlock. He’d been refused the keys by the building’s owner. Ainslie and his financial officer Matt Robinson managed to leave the building through the fire escape.

Industry observers note that ineos were applying petrochemicals business methods to sport, as usual. Fellows had also been employed by Ratcliffe to provide security assistance amid protests at Ineos’ controversial British fracking sites. The experienced security industry executive observed that ‘a small hard core group of activists’ was at work and that social media surveillance was useful, according to court papers from an earlier case.

Ineos denied the ‘false imprisonment’ of Ainslie, insisting that their employee had padlocked the building to prevent anyone entering, not knowing that someone was inside and that, in any case, there were ‘alternative exit routes’.

But the company did not entirely challenge Ainslie’s claim that Rob Nevin, chairman of Ratcliffe’s sports division and a Manchester United board member, had told him during a heated meeting about the disputed boat in Barcelona: ‘We have a phrase at Ineos: scorched earth. It means that if you don’t give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down, or words to that effect.’.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe's relationship with his one-time friend Ben Ainslie ruptured after Ineos withdrew support for the latter's America’s Cup bid.

Ratcliffe's running of Manchester United is criticised by one anonymous source. ‘People like him see football on TV and just assume they can do it,’ they say.

That threat, which Ineos say was only made figuratively, illustrates how Ratcliffe runs his businesses with what several sources describe as a cult-like authority, full of such maxims and mantras laid down to staff who fear him.

That ‘cult of Sir Jim’ is born of the billionaire’s own immense air of superiority and is something he seems to have instilled in some of his most senior executives.

Recent findings suggest that nevin, 68, a long-standing Ratcliffe lieutenant, has informed some who have encountered him since he arrived at Old Trafford that he has completed 60 or more major ‘transactions’ – business deals – in the oil and gas industry. He is described as ‘not short on confidence’.

Nevin chairs Ineos Sport, the collection of acquisitions built up when Ratcliffe believed his firm could straddle multiple sports and succeed at all of them, in the style of Red Bull. Ratcliffe disastrously installed his brother, Bob, as chief executive at OGC Nice, the second of the football teams he bought, and that air of superiority and ‘always knowing’ has been manifest at United, too.

Recent findings suggest that ratcliffe demonstrated to some of the Manchester United players the stretches he was using for London Marathon training, after buying the club. He considered his friend Sir Dave Brailsford to be ‘best in class’ when it came to running the football side of the club, despite the former Team Sky cycling chief only having a loose connection of football contacts, mostly picked up from his appearances on the Leaders in Sport conference circuit for his friend Jimmy Worrall, the entrepreneur who set up that business.

Sources have told us that Brailsford was so enamoured with Manchester City, after arriving to ‘save United’, that he and other Ineos people were ‘skipping around’ when Omar Berrada, chief operations officer at the Etihad, was hired as chief executive.

‘There was no sense from Ratcliffe of needing people who understand the industry and its craft,’ claims one source, speaking on condition of anonymity. ‘People like this see football on TV and just assume they can do it.’.

Ratcliffe (pictured next to former United boss Erik ten Hag) inexplicably considered Dave Brailsford (right) to be ‘best in class’ when it came to running the football side of the club.

Rob Nevin (right) chairs Ineos Sport, the collection of acquisitions built up when Ratcliffe wrongly believed his firm could straddle multiple sports and succeed at all of them.

None of Ratcliffe’s executives will be wanting to tell him that. A further sense of what a formidable presence he is for his own staff came in a 30-minute ‘Ask Jim’ interview with him, conducted by his own director of corporate affairs, Tom Crotty, this summer.

Ratcliffe stares at the floor for much of the time as Crotty bowls him a series of long-hop questions and he seems profoundly miserable, revealing little more than his unhappiness with the British government’s management of North Sea oilfields and his dislike for the British sports press.

The interview was conducted the day after the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina in July, which Ratcliffe attended. ‘It was fabulous. A great celebration, despite the whining British press who really didn’t like it,’ he says.

Asked how he switches off, he cites time on the golf driving range and fishing on his salmon farm in Iceland – to which Berrada and the Glazers have had to make their way for some executive meetings. ‘Biggest lessons learned in 2025?’ There don’t appear to have been any. At no stage do United feature.

Ratcliffe trots out his extremely well-worn mantra about the major three traits Ineos prize most – ‘Grit, rigour, humour’ – informing the relentlessly positive Crotty of the need to ‘do work properly before you make important decisions, because you need to spend capital well.’.

According to recent reports, that’s not happened in sport. The extraordinary rupture with Ainslie, after Ineos withdrew support for a third America’s Cup cycle and he continued to use the boat, is part of a general, hugely acrimonious winding down of the Ineos Sport masterplan.

OGC Nice and FC Lausanne-Sport, Ratcliffe’s European football clubs, are up for sale amid fan protest, while it is widely expected that Ineos will eventually disappear from cycling. They have already diluted their involvement, with the team formerly known as the Ineos Grenadiers now co-sponsored by Danish technology firm Netcompany. The All Blacks and Tottenham Hotspur both sued Ineos for prematurely terminating commercial relationships. Both parties ultimately reached a confidential legal settlement with the company.

What United need, as they look to Mauricio Pochettino for deliverance, is for Ratcliffe to climb down from his lofty peak, display some of the humility which has been missing and admit there have been faults.

What United need, as they look to Mauricio Pochettino for deliverance, is for Ratcliffe to display some humility.

The club's executives, including CEO Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox (right), have appeared out of their depth and in need of support.

The view among some outsiders who interact at a high level with the club is, in the words of one, that United are ‘the biggest club in the world and yet no longer the biggest club in the world'. They carry huge expectation, yet are unable to compete for transfer fees and wages with Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City, and have removed excellent staff without replacing them. To cite only one, Victoria Timpson secured the club’s lucrative Snapdragon sponsorship deal but still departed.

‘If United were an iPhone, someone would need to unfold the paper clip pretty quick, push it in the side of the phone and hard restart everything,’ says the aforementioned source. 'The club need a genuinely industry-leading chief executive, a sporting director of the calibre of Edwin van der Sar who, unlike Jason Wilcox, has the experience, pedigree and knowledge he accumulated as CEO at Ajax. They need a boardroom presence and link to the fans like Bryan Robson.'.

Ratcliffe does not even sit on the United board himself, leaving it to Nevin and John Reece, one of the Ineos co-founders.

Recent findings suggest that another of his Ineos appointees was the 63-year-old Frenchman Jean-Claude Blanc, an experienced statesman and marketeer with an Olympic, Tour de France and PSG background, who is described as pleasant and without ego – though he was supposedly in the room when the 'scorched' earth comment was made to Ainslie. Blanc was recruited for his gravitas, rather than to pull up trees. He has stepped down from United's board.

Industry observers note that ainslie and Ratcliffe are no longer thought to be friends. Shortly before the alleged episode in the locked aerodrome building, Ainslie observed, in relation to Ratcliffe, that there was a difference between business and sport, where teams were delicately balanced, nuanced groups of people.

‘You want to save money and be efficient, but you’ve got to make sure you look after people. You need that balance,’ he said. Under the terms of the court settlement, Ainslie gets to keep the boat and sail off into the sunset, leaving Ratcliffe to whatever storms come next.

Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

Sources indicate that what a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Sources indicate that jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

Sources indicate that the lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the complications Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Industry observers note that thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

According to recent reports, the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

Industry observers note that what they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

Sources indicate that the roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Sources indicate that hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

It must be noted the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

In a recent development, the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton tasted their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup as the Blues' four-game winning streak in the competition came to its conclusion with a 2-1 defeat away to Manchester United.

First half strikes from Mared Griffiths and Emma Watson put the Red Devils in to a two-goal lead, before Noemie Mouchon halved the deficit two minutes after the break.

Prior to Wednesday night's clash, the Toffees had comfortably beaten Birmingham City, Newcastle United and Sheffield United before thrashing Durham 6-0 in the competition.

Head coach Scott Phelan named a heavily-rotated XI from the side that were held to a goalless draw against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.

Rylee Foster-Inman started in between the sticks, with Issy Hobson making her first appearance in two months in front of her.

Up top, Mouchon led the line after netting a brace in the Blues’ 6-0 demolition of Durham seven days ago.

Sources indicate that foster-Inman produced a fine save when faced one-on-one with Griffiths inside six minutes. The keeper rushed out upon recognising the danger and did brilliantly to narrow the angle.

The shot-stopper denied Griffiths once more on 21 minutes as the youngster pulled the trigger from the edge of the box after a cute turn saw her evade Hobson.

It has been revealed that the lively Griffiths was in the thick of the action once more in the 34th minute as United came inches away from opening the scoring. Rebecca Bernal burst forward to meet her in swinging cross, the Mexican’s header sailing just over.

Industry observers note that griffiths would not be denied only 60 seconds later as the forward broke the deadlock in style. She sprinted down the left before chopping past Finnigan and firing past the outrushed Foster-Inman.

In a recent development, watson then doubled the hosts’ lead on the stroke of half-time. Ella Toone wrong-footed Finnigan before pulling it back to the former-Blue. Watson finished emphatically from close range, with that concluding the action for the opening 45.

Defensive duo Hobson and Silcock made way for Hannah Blundell and Rion Ishikawa at the break.

Industry observers note that everton halved the deficit only 60 seconds after the restart as Mouchon netted her third goal from her last two Cup appearances. Quick feet from Vignola allowed the Spaniard room to free Hannah Cain down the right. The Wales international then squared it to the advancing Mouchon, who finished off the post.

It has been revealed that maz Pacheco then came agonisingly close from 20-yards out as her wicked free-kick rattled the upright. The full-back picked her spot from the set-piece – the ball crashing against the crossbar with the keeper well-beaten.

Phelan then made two further changes on 68 minutes as Ruby Mace and Hikaru Kitagawa replaced Clare Wheeler and Vignola.

With eight minutes remaining, Naomi Layzell – who claimed the Player of the Match award when the two sides met in the WSL – came on in place of Aurora Galli.

Despite a late push for an equaliser, United stood firm and succumbed the Toffees to their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup.
